test_text.title: How Much Higher? How Much Faster?

article.title: How Much Higher? How Much Faster?

items.sentence_raw: Since the early years of the twentieth century, when the International Athletic Federation began keeping records, there has been a steady improvement in how fast athletes run, how high they jump and how far they are able to hurl massive objects, themselves included, through space.
items.explain: Q1: The passage says records began *'when the International Athletic Federation began keeping records'* in the *'early years of the twentieth century'*. **'Early years of the twentieth century'** means around **1900**. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: For the so-called power events - that require a relatively brief, explosive release of energy, like the 100-metre sprint and the long jump - times and distances have improved ten to twenty percent.
items.explain: Q3: The question says improvement is **most** in events needing an *'intensive burst of energy'* — these are **power events**. But the passage says endurance events had *'more dramatic'* results, and power events improved only *'ten to twenty percent'*. So the statement is opposite to the passage — the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: In the endurance events the results have been more dramatic.
items.explain: Q3: The question says improvement is **most** in events needing an *'intensive burst of energy'* — these are **power events**. But the passage says endurance events had *'more dramatic'* results, and power events improved only *'ten to twenty percent'*. So the statement is opposite to the passage — the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: At the 1908 Olympics, John Hayes of the U.S. team ran a marathon in a time of 2:55:18.
In 1999, Morocco's Khalid Khannouchi set a new world record of 2:05:42, almost thirty percent faster.
No one theory can explain improvements in performance, but the most important factor has been genetics.
items.explain: Q4: The passage directly says *'No one theory can explain improvements'* — **'no one theory'** means it cannot be **fully** explained by just one thing. So saying genetics can **fully** explain it is wrong — the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: "The athlete must choose his parents carefully," says Jesus Dapena, a sports scientist at Indiana University, invoking an oft-cited adage.

Over the past century, the composition of the human gene pool has not changed appreciably, but with increasing global participation in athletics - and greater rewards to tempt athletes - it is more likely that individuals possessing the unique complement of genes for athletic performance can be identified early.
items.explain: Q6: The passage says with more global participation, talented individuals can be *'identified early'*. **'Identified early'** means the same as **'recognised at a younger age'**. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: "Was there someone like [sprinter] Michael Johnson in the 1920s?"
Dapena asks.
"I'm sure that there was, but his talent was probably never realized."
Identifying genetically talented individuals is only the first step.
Michael Yessis, an emeritus professor of Sports Science at California State University at Fullerton, maintains that "genetics only determines about one third of what an athlete can do.
But with the right training we can go much further with that one third than we've been going."
Yessis believes that U.S. runners, despite their impressive achievements, are "running on their genetics".
items.explain: Q7: Yessis says U.S. runners are *'running on their genetics'* — this means they rely on their natural **genetics** for success. So the answer is **genetics**.

items.sentence_raw: By applying more scientific methods, "they're going to go much faster".
These methods include strength training that duplicates what they are doing in their running events as well as plyometrics, a technique pioneered in the former Soviet Union.
Whereas most exercises are designed to build up strength or endurance, plyometrics focuses on increasing power - the rate at which an athlete can expend energy.
items.explain: Q8: The passage says plyometrics *'focuses on increasing power'* — this is the specific aim of that Soviet training method. So the answer is **power**.

items.sentence_raw: When a sprinter runs, Yessis explains, her foot stays in contact with the ground for just under a tenth of a second, half of which is devoted to landing and the other half to pushing off.
Plyometric exercises help athletes make the best use of this brief interval.
Nutrition is another area that sports trainers have failed to address adequately.
"Many athletes are not getting the best nutrition, even through supplements," Yessis insists.
Each activity has its own nutritional needs.
Few coaches, for instance, understand how deficiencies in trace mineral can lead to injuries.
items.explain: Q9: Yessis says *'deficiencies in trace mineral can lead to injuries'* — an inadequate diet means not enough minerals, which links directly to **injuries**. So the answer is **injuries**.

items.sentence_raw: Focused training will also play a role in enabling records to be broken.
items.explain: Q10: The passage states *'Focused training will also play a role in enabling records to be broken'* — better **training** is the key. So the answer is **training**.

items.sentence_raw: "If we applied the Russian training model to some of the outstanding runners we have in this country," Yessis asserts, "they would be breaking records left and right."

He will not predict by how much, however: "Exactly what the limits are it's hard to say, but there will be increase even if only by hundredths of a second, as long as our training continues to improve."
One of the most important new methodologies is biomechanics, the study of the body in motion.
A biomechanics films an athlete in action and then digitizes her performance, recording the motion of every joint and limb in three dimensions.

By applying Newton's laws to these motions, "we can say that this athlete's run is not fast enough; that this one is not using his arms strongly enough during take-off," says Dapena, who uses these methods to help high jumpers.
items.explain: Q11: The passage says biomechanics can point out problems like a run *'not fast enough'* or arms *'not... strongly enough'* — this means they **highlight areas for improvement**. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: To date, however, biomechanics has made only a small difference to athletic performance.
Revolutionary ideas still come from the athletes themselves.

For example, during the 1968 Olympics in Mexico City, a relatively unknown high jumper named Dick Fosbury won the gold by going over the bar backwards, in complete contradiction of all the received high-jumping wisdom, a move instantly dubbed the Fosbury flop.
Fosbury himself did not know what he was doing.

That understanding took the later analysis of biomechanics, who put their minds to comprehending something that was too complex and unorthodox ever to have been invented through their own mathematical simulations.
items.explain: Q12: The passage says biomechanics specialists later worked on *'comprehending'* the Fosbury flop — **'comprehending'** means **explaining** it. ***Option B is a trap*** — they did not create it, the athlete did. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Fosbury also required another element that lies behind many improvements in athletic performance: an innovation in athletic equipment.
In Fosbury's case, it was the cushions that jumpers land on.
Traditionally, high jumpers would land in pits filled with sawdust.
But by Fosbury's time, sawdust pits had been replaced by soft foam cushions, ideal for flopping.
In the end, most people who examine human performance are humbled by the resourcefulness of athletes and the powers of the human body.
"Once you study athletics, you learn that it's a vexingly complex issue," says John S. Raglin, a sports psychologist at Indiana University.
"Core performance is not a simple or mundane thing of higher, faster, longer.
So many variables enter into the equation, and our understanding in many cases is fundamental.
items.explain: Q13: Raglin says our understanding *'in many cases is fundamental'* — **'fundamental'** here means **basic**, not advanced. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: We've got a long way to go."
For the foreseeable future, records will be made to be broken.

subtitles: Limits to Human Sporting Performance Are Not Yet in Sight

orphan_explain_map.2: Q2: The passage talks about improvement *'since the early years of the twentieth century'*, but it says nothing about performance **before** that time. We don't know if there was little improvement or a lot — the information is missing. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
orphan_explain_map.5: Q5: The passage mentions an adage about choosing parents carefully, but it never says that top athletes' parents **were** successful athletes themselves. This specific fact is not confirmed or denied anywhere. So the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
